# Results — Study 496 (Three-Line-Break)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **a
Three-Line-Break reversal forecasts a new trend: go long on the bullish 3-line up-break** —
encoded as a mechanical rule. TLB lines are built causally from past closes only; the chart
flips down→up only when the close breaks the highs of the **3** latest down-lines; a long fires
on that reversal bar, entered at the **next close** (one documented lag), and we measure the
forward 5/10/20/60-day return. Offline & deterministic once cached; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Entries | **943** mechanical 3-line up-reversals pooled across the 5 tapes (break number = 3) |
| Timing / costs | TLB reversal read on close of *t*; enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per reversal |

> **Price-only vs total-return.** The ETFs are auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested) — labelled
> total-return everywhere. The Signal axis uses a basket of **surviving** liquid ETFs; this is a
> single-instrument trend study, not a cross-sectional anomaly, so survivorship affects only the
> drift baseline (which is exactly what the random-entry control neutralizes).

## The signal — TLB up-reversal vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (it measures the index's upward drift); the
**Welch reversal-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ = reversal − random.

| horizon | n | reversal | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (rev−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 940 | +16.5 bps | 60% | +2.05 | +16.3 bps | **+0.2 bps** | +14.5 bps | +0.02 | 0.986 |
| 10-day | 940 | +31.9 bps | 61% | +2.59 | +60.3 bps | **−28.4 bps** | +29.9 bps | −1.79 | 0.073 |
| 20-day | 938 | +93.1 bps | 64% | +5.29 | +115.5 bps | **−22.4 bps** | +91.1 bps | −1.02 | 0.307 |
| 60-day | 932 | +258.4 bps | 69% | +6.26 | +290.9 bps | **−32.5 bps** | +256.4 bps | −0.89 | 0.373 |

Read it carefully. The one-sample *t* against zero looks excellent (**+5.29** at 20 days,
**+6.26** at 60) — but that is **pure beta**: long-only entries on an upward-drifting index
inherit the drift. Against the **drift-matched random baseline**, the TLB up-reversal is a
*tie* at 5 days (Δ = +0.2 bps) and *worse* at every longer horizon (Δ = −28.4 / −22.4 / −32.5
bps at 10/20/60 days). The reversal-minus-random difference **never clears the desk's *t* ≥ 2
bar** (max Welch *t* = +0.02 at 5 days; the longer horizons are negative). The 3-line reversal
does not forecast.

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — the reversal loses to random in 3 of 5

| ticker | entries | reversal | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (rev−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 211 | +114.1 bps | +3.63 | +145.2 bps | **−31.1 bps** |
| QQQ | 210 | +87.6 bps | +2.17 | +165.9 bps | **−78.3 bps** |
| IWM | 183 | +49.6 bps | +0.96 | +93.3 bps | **−43.7 bps** |
| DIA | 193 | +91.4 bps | +2.97 | +88.2 bps | **+3.2 bps** |
| GLD | 146 | +127.4 bps | +3.20 | +64.2 bps | **+63.2 bps** |

Only **GLD** shows a meaningful positive delta (+63.2 bps) and DIA a marginal one (+3.2 bps);
in 3 of 5 names the famous reversal *underperforms* a random-day entry — and even the single
positive case (GLD) does not survive pooling, where the Welch test is flat. No coherent
cross-sectional edge — the hallmark of relabelled drift.

## Geometry placebo — scramble the line-break sequence, nothing changes

The decisive "does the line-break geometry matter?" test: keep the **same daily returns** (so
the price marginal, drift and volatility are unchanged) but permute their **order**, so the
specific sequence of breaks that strings runs into a 3-line reversal becomes meaningless. If the
reversal genuinely forecast, the scramble would collapse the result.

| test | observed up-reversal 20d return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY shuffled-returns TLB | +114.1 bps | **0.261** | 500 |

**26% of scrambled-sequence tapes match or beat the real one** (*p* = 0.261). The specific
line-break geometry carries no extra information beyond the return marginal — a randomly
reordered tape reverses just as profitably. "The 3-line reversal forecasts" is busted.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real continuation

On a deterministic tape with a *planted* post-reversal continuation (knob `edge`: a ~20-session
positive drift burst injected right after each genuine 3-line up-reversal), the same TLB rule
behaves exactly as it must — so the flat real-tape result is a genuine "nothing there", not a
dead detector.

| planted edge | n | reversal | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no continuation) | 138 | −2.0 bps | 49% | −0.05 |
| **0.60** (real planted continuation) | 84 | +617.4 bps | 76% | **+6.13** |

With no planted continuation the control sits at *t* ≈ 0 (no false positive); a real planted
continuation lights up at *t* = +6.13 with a 76% win-rate. The detector is live.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The TLB up-reversal does **not** beat a drift-matched random baseline
  (reversal − random = +0.2 / −28.4 / −22.4 / −32.5 bps at 5/10/20/60 days; the Welch *t* never
  clears 2, max +0.02 at 5 days, *p* = 0.986). The impressive one-sample *t*'s (20-day +5.29,
  60-day +6.26) are pure beta — the upward drift of long equity indices.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is no residual edge once the drift you were always getting is
  removed, and costs only deepen the hole. The same drift is captured more cheaply and more
  fully by holding the index; the reversal rule trades less and pays costs on each signal,
  dominating nothing. No capacity question because there is no edge to scale.
- **"Does the 3-line reversal forecast?" — BUSTED.** The shuffled-returns placebo leaves the
  result intact (*p* = 0.261): a randomly reordered tape reverses just as profitably, so the
  specific Three-Line-Break geometry carries no forecasting information. TLB is a descriptive
  noise-filter chart, not a forecasting strategy.
